nameStory: This bee gets its "sculptured" name from the intricate, carved-looking patterns on its body that resemble fine metalwork or carved stone. The "resin" part comes from its remarkable building skills - it collects tree resin and plant materials to construct waterproof nests, like a tiny architect working with natural glue.
description: The Sculptured Resin Bee is a robust, impressive native bee that's one of the larger bees you'll encounter in New England. These chunky, dark-bodied bees have a somewhat rough, textured appearance with distinctive sculptured patterns across their bodies. They're solitary bees, meaning each female builds and provisions her own nest rather than living in a hive like honeybees. You'll often see them busily collecting materials to build their resin-based nests in hollow stems or small cavities.

idTips.label: Sculptured body texture
idTips.description: The body surface has distinctive carved or etched-looking patterns that feel rough to the touch, like fine sandpaper, giving it a metalworked appearance

idTips.label: Large, robust size
idTips.description: Noticeably chunky and substantial compared to most other native bees, with a heavy, solid feel if handled

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Predominantly dark brown to black body with minimal light markings, appearing almost charcoal-colored in good light

idTips.label: Thick, powerful mandibles
idTips.description: Large, prominent jaws that look capable of serious cutting work, often visible even when the bee is at rest

idTips.label: Behavioral clues
idTips.description: Often seen carrying visible chunks of resin or plant material, flying with a purposeful, heavy flight pattern

habitat: Look for Sculptured Resin Bees in gardens, parks, and forest edges where they can find both flowering plants and suitable nesting sites. They prefer areas with dead wood, bamboo, or hollow plant stems where they can excavate nest tunnels. You'll often spot them near conifers and deciduous trees where they collect resin, especially in suburban and semi-urban environments with mixed native and ornamental plantings.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring and start establishing territories. Look for them investigating potential nesting sites in dead wood or hollow stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you'll see them most actively foraging for pollen, nectar, and resin materials. This is the best time to observe their distinctive building behaviors.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall as late-season adults finish provisioning nests. Some individuals may still be active on warm autumn days.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off and the species overwinters as developing larvae in their resin-sealed nest cells, completely hidden from view.

funFact: These bees are such skilled architects that they can chew through mortar and soft brick to create their nest tunnels, sometimes causing minor damage to buildings - they're like tiny living power drills with wings!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with carpenter bees, but carpenter bees have shiny, hairless abdomens that look almost polished, while Sculptured Resin Bees have that distinctive rough, textured body surface. Remember: smooth and shiny = carpenter bee, rough and sculptured = resin bee.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "resin bees," they're actually more closely related to leafcutter bees and use similar construction techniques, just substituting resin for cut leaves. This species is native to Asia but has become established in parts of North America, representing an interesting example of how bee species can adapt to new environments.
compareHints: Unlike the leafcutter bees in its genus that cut neat circular pieces from leaves, the Sculptured Resin Bee collects sticky tree resins and other plant materials for nest construction. It's significantly larger and more robust than most other Megachile species, and lacks the clean leaf-cutting behavior that gives its relatives their name. While other resin bees in the genus tend to be smaller and more delicately built, this species has a distinctly chunky, powerful appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's leafcutter bees, males of this species are easily distinguished by their notably broad front legs - most other Megachile males have normal-width legs.
Among New England's many Megachile species, the Alfalfa Leafcutter Bee is distinguished by its agricultural associations and widespread management by farmers.

Among New England's many Megachile species, the Flat-tailed Leafcutter's compressed abdomen sets it apart from relatives like the Alfalfa Leafcutter Bee and Patchwork Leafcutter Bee, which have more typically rounded abdomens.
Unlike the leaf-cutting members of its genus like the patchwork leafcutter bee, the bellflower resin bee works exclusively with sticky materials and never cuts leaf pieces.
Among New England's leafcutter bees, the Pugnacious stands out for its completely black coloration and larger size - most relatives have some lighter markings or metallic hints.
Compared to other Megachile species, unarmed leafcutter bees are distinguished by the males' lack of prominent facial or leg spines that many relatives possess.

Among New England's many Megachile species, the Golden-tailed Leafcutter Bee stands out with its distinctive golden abdominal hairs, while relatives like the Black-and-gray Leafcutter Bee have contrasting gray and black coloration instead.
